title: Upgrade canary rollback decision tree and health probes
body:
Purpose:
This working doc captures a lightweight, operationally-safe decision tree for canary upgrades (VPC/on-prem PRIVATE deployments), a minimal set of health probes/smoke-tests to gate progressive rollout, and Terraform gating notes to reduce bad upgrades. It is intended for SREs and site owners running dedicated/private stacks; treat as a pre-flight checklist + triage playbook for the first 15 minutes after an anomalous canary.

High-level goals:
- Detect regressions that matter in production within 3 minutes of canary traffic
- Fail fast and rollback automatically for class-A failures (data loss, crashloops, severe latency regressions)
- Continue canary when only class-B minor degradations occur (single-route error spike, metric regressions below threshold)
- Provide clear runbook steps and Terraform gating to avoid partial incompatible TF changes

Definitions and assumption:
- Canary group: a small fraction of machines (5% or one availability zone) running the new image/configuration.
- Control group: remaining fleet serving production.
- Health window: 3 minutes for per-request checks, 30 minutes for stability observation.
- Class-A failure: node crashloops, persistent OOMs on runtime, KV-cache corruption detected, replication break, or >50% error-rate on 10k requests aggregated within 3 min.
- Class-B failure: latency p95 increase >25% vs baseline, spike in transient errors <10% of traffic, or slow backend dependencies.

Quick canary rollout decision tree (operational steps):
1) Start canary: Deploy to canary pool (k8s nodeSelector + tf module target). Start 1m low-traffic smoke routing (10–50 rps).
2) Immediate probes (0–3m): run the "must-pass" smoke suite (see probes below). If any must-pass probe fails -> mark class-A and trigger rollback (automated).
3) If immediate probes pass, continue 30m observation under realistic load. Aggregate latency, error-rate, OOMs, and resource usage. Use the gating thresholds below.
4) At 30m: if metrics are within thresholds -> expand to 25% rollout and repeat canary checks. If class-B anomalies observed -> hold and run targeted diagnostics; escalate to engineers if questionable.
5) Any node-level fatality (GPU driver mismatch, kernel panic, mount failures) -> immediate rollback + create postmortem ticket.

Must-pass (blocking) probes — fast (0–3 min):
- Control vs canary smoke: send identical 200 synthetic requests to canary and control; require identical status codes and structured output signature checks for >95% of requests.
- Startup sanity: all service containers in canary pod must be Running and Ready within 90s. (kubectl -n redwood get pods -l canary=true -o wide)
- KV cache boot: request a tokenized prefix twice; second request must be served from cache (verify via X-Cache: HIT header or internal metric).
- Model loading: monitor model loaded event in logs ("model load complete") per process within 120s and no repeated load/unload loops.
- Basic inference latency: p50 < baseline p50 * 2 and p95 < baseline p95 * 1.5 for 200 probes.
- Resource sanity: no OOMKilled or CrashLoopBackOff in canary pods.

Non-blocking (observational) probes — 0–30 min:
- End-to-end latency histograms compared to control (p50/p95/p99 thresholds).
- Error budgets per route (20-minute rolling window).
- File-system mounts: check NFS/CEPH mount latency and file read success rates; transient mount errors acceptable but repeated failures are blocking.
- GPU driver logs: check for "cuda driver mismatch" strings in dmesg/syslog.

Terraform module gating notes (practical rules):
- No simultaneous TF changes to runtime and networking modules in the same plan. Split into separate applies staged by time.
- Use terraform plan -out=plan.tfout and review plan diff for module.module_name.resource_name replacements. If resource will be recreated instead of updated, flag for manual review.
- For module version bumps: pin new module version in a feature branch and run an infra-canary apply to a non-prod mirror (or to a single dedicated dev node) first.
- Avoid changing provider versions (kubernetes/helm/aws) during an upgrade unless accompanied by a compatibility test matrix.
- When modifying node labels/tolerations used for routing (example: nodeSelector: redwood-serving=true), ensure the rollout includes a transitional label step: 1) add transitional label -> 2) attach pods to both selectors -> 3) remove old selector. This reduces transient 0-capacity windows.

Automated rollback triggers (examples):
- Any must-pass probe failure -> immediate rollback.
- Error-rate >50% on any route for >2 consecutive minutes.
- >3% on-call paged resource errors (OOMs, cpu saturation >95% for >5 minutes) on canary nodes.
- Repeated model load failures (>=3 restarts in 10 minutes).

Triage checklist (first 15 minutes after a failing canary):
- Step 0: Capture the state snapshot: kubectl -n redwood get pods, kubectl -n redwood describe pod <pod>, kubectl -n redwood logs -f <pod> --since=15m. Save to ephemeral artifact S3.
- Step 1: Compare canary vs control logs for first error timestamp. grep for "model load", "cache corrupt", "OOMKilled", "traceback".
- Step 2: Check node-level dmesg and system logs for driver/kernel messages.
- Step 3: Run terraform state list | grep module.runtime to ensure changed resources map to expected new instances. If resources are being recreated unexpectedly, abort and rollback.
- Step 4: Snapshot persistent volume mounts (df -h; mount; ls -la /mnt/model-store). If mounts are stale or readonly, that indicates FS compatibility regression.
- Step 5: Confirm GPU driver and container runtime: nvidia-smi, docker info | grep cgroup; verify cgroup v1 vs v2 mismatch causes.

Common failure patterns and rapid hypotheses:
- Symptom: model process exits shortly after startup. Hypothesis: model binary linked to newer CUDA than node driver. Check: nvidia-smi driver version vs binary reported CUDA compatibility. Fix: pin runtime image to matching driver ABI or upgrade node driver.
- Symptom: sudden p95 explosion with normal p50. Hypothesis: slow tail due to KV cache warming; check cache hit-rate and background eviction. Fix: pre-warm cache or increase cache reservation during canary.
- Symptom: localized 502s from ingress. Hypothesis: headless service DNS resolution flapping after pod evictions. Check kube-proxy logs, CoreDNS. Fix: increase DNS TTL and reduce pod churn.
- Symptom: TF apply recreating nodes. Hypothesis: immutable bootstrap resource changed (instance_id, disk name). Check plan for replace/taint operations. Fix: rework module to use lifecycle.ignore_changes or use a migration apply path.

Runbook snippets (commands to collect quickly):
- kubectl -n redwood get pods -l canary=true -o wide --show-labels
- kubectl -n redwood logs <pod> --since=10m --tail=200
- kubectl -n redwood exec -it <pod> -- curl -sS -D - -o /dev/null http://localhost:8080/health
- ssh node && sudo dmesg | tail -n 200
- terraform plan -out=plan.tfout && terraform show -json plan.tfout | jq '.resource_changes[] | {address,change: .change.actions}'

Post-incident notes and next steps (if rollback):
- Do not reapply identical change. Create a small hypothesis branch that isolates the suspected toggle (image, env, tf module). Reproduce in a dev mirror.
- Produce a minimal repro test for the failing probe and add it to the smoke suite.
- If Terraform caused replace operations, add a lifecycle ignore_changes for the resource until a planned migration path is created.

Appendix: Minimal canary smoke suite (to be executed by the CI canary job)
- probe-01-basic-infer.sh: 200 short prompts, verify 98% non-empty outputs and status 200
- probe-02-persistent-storage.sh: write/read 10MB file to model store mount
- probe-03-concurrent-burst.sh: 50 parallel requests ramping to 500 RPS for 30s and check p95 < threshold
- probe-04-cache-hit-check.py: two identical requests; assert second served from cache header

Feedback and next iterations:
- This doc should be converted to a decision-tree in the runbook UI and wired into the automated canary controller.
